facts.text: Arenas Valley got its name from the Rio de Arenas, a dry arroyo that locals once called Whiskey Creek after a flood carried whiskey barrels down it.
Near Arenas Valley lies the Santa Rita del Cobre mine, one of the oldest copper mines in the U.S., operating since the early 1800s.
Before European arrival, the Apache people used the Arenas Valley area for hunting, gathering, and seasonal movement across the Southwest.
Although mining activity has faded, the legacy remains in local landmarks, shaping Arenas Valley’s quiet residential identity amid desert landscapes.
Arenas Valley sits within the Gila National Forest, giving residents easy access to the world’s first designated wilderness area, the Gila Wilderness.
In 1800, an Apache guide showed Spanish officer José Manuel Carrasco the Santa Rita copper mines, sparking early European interest in the area.
